summary.title: Write more "useless" software
summary.one_liner: Building playful, purposeless programs for fun and learning can rekindle joy in coding and teach real technical skills.
takeaways: Writing software purely for play frees you from obligations and lets you define your own goals.
Useless projects can teach real skills, such as GUI and game programming, systems programming, protocols, and interpreters.
Work pressures can drain the enjoyment of programming, so playful projects help keep the spark alive.
You can stop a playful project at any time, skip tests or tooling, and abandon it when it stops being fun.
summary.summary: The author, responding to a question about why he wrote Hurl, argues that building 'useless' software is a valuable form of play that restores joy in programming. He explains that daily work obligations can drain enthusiasm, while personal projects let you set your own scope and stop whenever you like. He lists examples of his own playful projects, including a chess engine and UI, a Redis-like key-value store, a wake-on-LAN utility, a POP3 server implementation, and work through Crafting Interpreters and Mazes for Programmers. The post is a short, personal essay with a footnote recommending the Recurse Center.
